<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label[theorem]{thm:musin}
Let $m\geq1$ and $1\leq n\leq k\leq d$. If
\begin{equation}\label{eq:musin-criterion}
 P_{k,n}^{\,m}\notin
 (x_1^{d+1},x_2^d,\dots,x_k^{d-k+2}),
\end{equation}
then every collection of $m$ measures in $\mathbb{R}^d$ admits an
orthogonal $(k,n)$-equipartition. In particular,
$\Delta^*(m,k,n)\leq d$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label[theorem]{thm:main}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
 \item For every $j\geq1$,
 \[
  d^*(2^j-1,4,3)
  =R(2^j-1,4,3)
  =7\cdot2^{j-1}-2.
 \]

 \item If
 \[
  m=2^{q+1}(2^j-1)+r,
  \qquad
  j\geq1,\quad q\geq0,\quad 0\leq r\leq2^q-1,
 \]
 then
 \[
  d^*(m,4,3)
  =2^{q+1}\bigl(7\cdot2^{j-1}-2\bigr)+r.
 \]

 \item The equality $d^*(m,4,3)=R(m,4,3)$ holds if and only if
 $m=2^j-1$ for some $j\geq1$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label[corollary]{cor:geometric-dyadic}
For every $j\geq1$,
\[
 \Delta^*(2^j-1,4,3)=7\cdot2^{j-1}-2.
\]
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label[lemma]{lem:vdm}
For $k\geq2$,
\[
 Q_{k,1}Q_{k,2}=m_{(k,k-1,\dots,1)}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Over $\mathbb{F}_2$, the Vandermonde identity gives
$Q_{k,2}=m_{(k-1,k-2,\dots,0)}$.
Multiplication by $Q_{k,1}=x_1\cdots x_k$ yields the claim.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label[lemma]{lem:distinct}
Let $\lambda$ be a strict partition and $\pi$ a partition. Then every monomial of $m_\lambda m_\pi$ has pairwise distinct exponents; that is, $m_\lambda m_\pi$ is a sum of $m_\theta$ with $\theta$ a strict partition.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
For a partition $\gamma \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq0}^k$, $m_\gamma = \sum\limits_{\alpha \in S_k\gamma}x^\alpha$ as defined above, hence
\[
 m_\lambda m_\pi = \sum_{\alpha \in S_k\lambda}\sum_{\beta \in S_k\pi}x^{\alpha + \beta},
\]
and over $\mathbb{F}_2$ the coefficient of $x^\theta$ is the parity of the number of elements of
\[
 N(\theta) := \bigl\{(\alpha, \beta) \in S_k\lambda \times S_k\pi : \alpha + \beta = \theta\bigr\}.
\]
Let $\theta_i = \theta_j$ for some $i \neq j$, let $\tau \in S_k$ be the transposition of $i$ and $j$, and consider the map $(\alpha, \beta) \mapsto (\tau\alpha, \tau\beta)$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
 \item It maps $N(\theta)$ into itself: $\tau\alpha \in S_k\lambda$, $\tau\beta \in S_k\pi$, and $\tau\alpha + \tau\beta = \tau\theta = \theta$ because $\theta_i = \theta_j$.
 \item Applied twice, it is the identity.
 \item It has no fixed points: $\tau\alpha = \alpha$ would mean $\alpha_i = \alpha_j$, while the entries of $\alpha$, a rearrangement of the strict partition $\lambda$, are pairwise distinct.
\end{enumerate}
So $N(\theta)$ splits into pairs $\{(\alpha, \beta), (\tau\alpha, \tau\beta)\}$, $|N(\theta)|$ is even, and $[x^\theta](m_\lambda m_\pi) = 0$. Thus every monomial $x^\theta$ of $m_\lambda m_\pi$ has pairwise distinct exponents. As $m_\lambda m_\pi$ is symmetric, it is the sum of the $m_\theta$ over the partitions $\theta$ with $x^\theta$ a monomial of $m_\lambda m_\pi$, and these $\theta$ are strict partitions.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label[corollary]{cor:distinct}
Let $k \geq n \geq 2$ and $m \geq 1$. Then every monomial of $P_{k, n}^m$ has pairwise distinct exponents; that is, $P_{k, n}^m$ is a sum of $m_\theta$ with $\theta$ a strict partition.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Each $Q_{k, j}$ is symmetric, since a permutation of the variables permutes its factors. Write
\[
 P_{k, n}^m = Q_{k, 1}Q_{k, 2}F, \qquad F := Q_{k, 1}^{m - 1}Q_{k, 2}^{m - 1}Q_{k, 3}^m\cdots Q_{k, n}^m,
\]
where $F$ is symmetric, i.e., a sum of some $m_\pi$, and $Q_{k, 1}Q_{k, 2} = m_{(k, \dots, 2, 1)}$ with $(k, \dots, 2, 1)$ a strict partition (\Cref{lem:vdm}). By \Cref{lem:distinct}, every product $m_{(k, \dots, 2, 1)}m_\pi$ has only monomials with pairwise distinct exponents, and hence so does their sum $P_{k, n}^m$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
Throughout the rest of the paper, put $P:=P_{4,3}$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label[proposition]{prp:P}
We have
\[
 P=m_{(7,4,2,1)}+m_{(6,5,2,1)}
   +m_{(6,4,3,1)}+m_{(5,4,3,2)}.
\]
Consequently, every
$\pi\in\operatorname{supp} P$ has pairwise distinct entries in $[1,7]$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $e_i$ denote the elementary symmetric polynomials in four
variables and $s:=e_1$. Then
\[
 Q_{4,3}
 =\prod_{\ell=1}^4(s+x_\ell)
 =s^4+e_1s^3+e_2s^2+e_3s+e_4
 =e_1^2e_2+e_1e_3+e_4.
\]
Since
\[
 e_1^2e_2=m_{(3,1)}+m_{(2,1,1)},
 \qquad
 e_1e_3=m_{(2,1,1)},
\]
we obtain $Q_{4,3}=m_{(3,1)}+m_{(1,1,1,1)}$. Hence (\Cref{lem:vdm})
\[
 P=m_{(4,3,2,1)}
   \bigl(m_{(3,1)}+m_{(1,1,1,1)}\bigr).
\]

To expand $m_{(4,3,2,1)}m_{(3,1)}$, add each of the twelve
permutations of $(3,1,0,0)$ to $(4,3,2,1)$.
After sorting, the vectors with distinct entries give
$(7,4,2,1)$, $(6,5,2,1)$, and $(6,4,3,1)$ once each,
and $(5,4,3,2)$ twice (vectors with repeated entries can be ignored by \Cref{lem:distinct}). Thus
\[
 m_{(4,3,2,1)}m_{(3,1)}
 =m_{(7,4,2,1)}+m_{(6,5,2,1)}+m_{(6,4,3,1)}.
\]
Finally,
$m_{(4,3,2,1)}m_{(1,1,1,1)}=m_{(5,4,3,2)}$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label[corollary]{cor:truncation}
For $m\geq1$ and $d\geq4$,
\[
 P^m\notin(x_1^{d+1},x_2^{d+1},x_3^{d+1},x_4^{d+1})
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 P^m\notin(x_1^{d+1},x_2^d,x_3^{d-1},x_4^{d-2}).
\]
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
For the forward implication, symmetry and
\Cref{cor:distinct} allow us to order a surviving exponent
vector as $\theta_1>\cdots>\theta_4$. Then
$\theta_i\leq d-i+1$, so the corresponding monomial survives
the second truncation. The reverse implication is immediate.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
Write $d^*(m):=d^*(m,4,3)$ and
$R_j:=R(2^j-1,4,3)=7\cdot2^{j-1}-2$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label[proposition]{thm:lower}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
 \item $d^*(m)\geq R(m,4,3)$ for every $m\geq1$.
 \item Let $\lambda$ and $\pi = (t, t - 1, t - 2, t - 3)$ be strict partitions with $|\lambda| = |\pi|$ and $\lambda \neq \pi$. Then $\lambda_1 > t$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
(i) Take $\theta \in \operatorname{supp} P^m$ with $\max_i\theta_i = d^*(m)$. By \Cref{cor:distinct}, after reordering $\theta$ is a strict partition, so $\theta_i \leq \theta_1 - (i - 1)$ and
\[
 14m = |\theta| \leq \sum_{i = 1}^4\bigl(\theta_1 - (i - 1)\bigr) = 4d^*(m) - 6.
\]
Hence $d^*(m) \geq \frac{7m}{2} + \frac32$, and $d^*(m) \geq R(m, 4, 3)$ since $d^*(m)$ is an integer.

(ii) Assume $\lambda_1 \leq t$. Since $\lambda \neq \pi$ and $|\lambda| = |\pi|$, $\lambda$ is not an arithmetic progression with step $-1$ (such a progression is determined by its sum), so $\lambda_{s + 1} < \lambda_s - 1$ for some $s$. Thus $\lambda_i \leq \lambda_1 - (i - 1)$ for all $i$, strictly for $i = s + 1$, and
\[
 |\pi| = \sum_{i = 1}^4\bigl(t - (i - 1)\bigr) \geq \sum_{i = 1}^4\bigl(\lambda_1 - (i - 1)\bigr) > \sum_{i = 1}^4\lambda_i = |\lambda|,
\]
a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
Over $\mathbb{F}_2$, the Frobenius identity gives, for every $F\in\mathbb{F}_2[x_1,\dots,x_4]$,
\begin{equation}\label{prp:frob}
 F(x_1,\dots,x_4)^2=F(x_1^2,\dots,x_4^2).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label[corollary]{cor:double}
For every $m\geq1$, $d^*(2m)=2d^*(m)$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
By \eqref{prp:frob},
$\operatorname{supp} P^{2m}=\{2\theta:\theta\in\operatorname{supp} P^m\}$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label[lemma]{lem:drop}
For $1\leq m\leq m'$,
\[
 d^*(m)+(m'-m)\leq d^*(m').
\]
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Choose $\theta\in\operatorname{supp} P^{m'}$ with
$\max_i\theta_i=d^*(m')$. Since $P^{m'}=P^mP^{m'-m}$,
there exist $\varphi\in\operatorname{supp} P^m$ and
$\psi\in\operatorname{supp} P^{m'-m}$ such that $\theta=\varphi+\psi$.
As $\psi_i\geq m'-m$,
\[
 d^*(m)\leq\max_i\varphi_i
 \leq d^*(m')-(m'-m).
\]
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label[corollary]{cor:interval}
Let $1\leq a\leq b$. If
$d^*(b)\leq d^*(a)+b-a$, then
\[
 d^*(m)=d^*(a)+m-a
 \qquad\text{for every integer }a\leq m\leq b.
\]
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
By \Cref{lem:drop},
\[
 d^*(a)+m-a
 \leq d^*(m)
 \leq d^*(b)-(b-m)
 \leq d^*(a)+m-a.
\]
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
A \emph{frame} is a sequence $(X_q)$ in $\mathbb{Z}^4$, indexed by $q\geq0$ or $q\geq1$,
such that
\[
 X_{q+1}=2X_q,
 \qquad
 |X_q|=14\cdot2^q.
\]
A \emph{shape} is a vector $w\in\mathbb{Z}^4$ with $|w|=14$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
For a fixed frame, put
\[
 c_q(w):=[x^{X_q-w}]P^{2^q-1}.
\]
The degrees agree, since
$|X_q-w|=14(2^q-1)$. At level zero (if $X_0$ is defined),
$c_0(w)=1$ precisely when $w=X_0$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label[lemma]{lem:descent}
For every shape $w$ and $q\geq0$ whenever $X_q$ is defined,
\[
 c_{q+1}(w)
 =\sum_{\substack{\pi\in\operatorname{supp} P\ \pi\equiv w\pmod2}}
 c_q\left(\frac{w+\pi}{2}\right).
\]
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Put $N := 2^q - 1$. By the Frobenius identity (\Cref{prp:frob}),
\[
 P^{2N + 1} = P^N(x_1^2, \dots, x_4^2)\,P = \sum_{\theta \in \operatorname{supp} P^N} \sum_{\pi \in \operatorname{supp} P}x^{2\theta + \pi}.
\]
Since $X_{q + 1} = 2X_q$, the value $c_{q + 1}(w)$ is the number, mod $2$, of pairs $(\theta, \pi)$ in this double sum with $2\theta + \pi = 2X_q - w$ (there are none if $2X_q - w \notin \mathbb{Z}^4_{\geq0}$). 

For a given $\pi$, such a $\theta$ exists only if $\pi \equiv w \pmod 2$, and then it is unique: $\theta = X_q - v$ with $v := \frac{w + \pi}{2}$. This $v$ is a shape, since $|w| = |\pi| = 14$, and $X_q - v \in \operatorname{supp} P^N$ means exactly $c_q(v) = 1$. Summing over $\pi$ gives the formula.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label[lemma]{lem:sym}
If $\sigma\in S_4$ fixes the frame, then
$c_q(\sigma w)=c_q(w)$ for every $q\geq0$ whenever $X_q$ is defined.
If moreover $\sigma=(ij)$ and $w_i=w_j$, then
$c_q(w)=0$ for $q\geq1$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Put $N := 2^q - 1$ and $\theta := X_q - w$. Since $\sigma X_q = X_q$, we have $X_q - \sigma w = \sigma\theta$, so $c_q(\sigma w) = [x^{\sigma\theta}]P^N = [x^\theta]P^N = c_q(w)$, as $P^N$ is symmetric. 

If $\sigma = (ij)$, then $\sigma X_q = X_q$ means $(X_q)_i = (X_q)_j$, so $w_i = w_j$ gives $\theta_i = \theta_j$, and $c_q(w) = [x^\theta]P^N = 0$ by \Cref{cor:distinct} ($N \geq 1$ as $q \geq 1$).
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label[theorem]{thm:AP}
For every $q\geq1$,
\[
 c_q(\delta) = [x^{\theta_q}]P^{2^q-1} = 1.
\]
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
For $q=1$,
\[
 c_1(\delta)=[x^{(5,4,3,2)}]P=1
\]
by \Cref{prp:P}.

\Cref{lem:descent} gives
\[
 c_{q+1}(\delta)
 =\sum_{\substack{\pi\in\operatorname{supp} P\\
                  \pi\equiv(0,1,0,1)\pmod2}}
 c_q\left(\frac{\delta+\pi}{2}\right).
\]
Each partition in \Cref{prp:P} has two even and two odd
entries, so the sum has $16$ terms, listed below.
The shapes with distinct entries are shown in bold.
\[
\renewcommand{1.2}{1.2}
\begin{array}{c|cc|cc}
 \lambda
 & \pi & (\delta+\pi)/2
 & \pi & (\delta+\pi)/2\\ \hline
 (7,4,2,1)
 & (4,7,2,1) & (3,5,3,3)
 & (4,1,2,7) & (3,2,3,6)\\
 & (2,7,4,1) & \mathbf{(2,5,4,3)}
 & (2,1,4,7) & (2,2,4,6)\\ \hline
 (6,5,2,1)
 & (6,5,2,1) & (4,4,3,3)
 & (6,1,2,5) & \mathbf{(4,2,3,5)}\\
 & (2,5,6,1) & \mathbf{(2,4,5,3)}
 & (2,1,6,5) & (2,2,5,5)\\ \hline
 (6,4,3,1)
 & (6,3,4,1) & (4,3,4,3)
 & (6,1,4,3) & (4,2,4,4)\\
 & (4,3,6,1) & (3,3,5,3)
 & (4,1,6,3) & \mathbf{(3,2,5,4)}\\ \hline
 (5,4,3,2)
 & (4,5,2,3) & (3,4,3,4)
 & (4,3,2,5) & (3,3,3,5)\\
 & (2,5,4,3) & (2,4,4,4)
 & (2,3,4,5) & \mathbf{(2,3,4,5)}
\end{array}
\]
Eleven shapes have repeated entries and vanish by
\Cref{lem:sym}. The remaining five are permutations of
$\delta$. Since $X_q$ is invariant under $S_4$,
\Cref{lem:sym} gives
\[
 c_{q+1}(\delta)=5c_q(\delta)=c_q(\delta).
\]
Hence $c_q(\delta)=1$ for every $q\geq1$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label[corollary]{cor:dyadic}
For every $j\geq1$,
\[
 d^*(2^j-1)=R_j=7\cdot2^{j-1}-2.
\]
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
By \Cref{thm:AP}, the staircase monomial gives $d^*(2^j-1)\leq R_j$;
the reverse inequality is \Cref{thm:lower}(i).
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label[lemma]{lem:x1}
The monomials of $P$ in which $x_1$ has exponent $1$ are the $18$ monomials $x_1y^{2\sigma + \chi_l}$, where $\sigma$ runs over the permutations of $(1, 2, 3)$ and $l \in \{1, 2, 3\}$. Each vector $2\sigma + \chi_l$ has exactly one odd entry, at the place $l$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Since $x_1$ divides $P$, reduction modulo $x_1^2$ keeps exactly the monomials of $P$ with $x_1$-exponent $1$. As $Q_{4, 1} = x_1x_2x_3x_4$, we have $P = x_1F$ with $F := x_2x_3x_4\,Q_{4, 2}Q_{4, 3}$. Let $\bar F$ be the image of $F$ in $\mathbb{F}_2[x_1, \dots, x_4]/(x_1) \cong \mathbb{F}_2[y]$; then $F \equiv \bar F \pmod{x_1}$ gives $P \equiv x_1\bar F \pmod{x_1^2}$, and it remains to find $\bar F$. Below, $Q_{3, j}$ stands for $Q_{3, j}(y)$.

The polynomial $Q_{4, 2}$ is the product of six linear forms. Modulo $x_1$, the three forms $x_1 + x_j$ become $x_j$, with product $x_2x_3x_4 = Q_{3, 1}$, while the other three, $x_i + x_j$ with $2 \leq i < j \leq 4$, do not contain $x_1$ and form $Q_{3, 2}$; so $Q_{4, 2} \equiv Q_{3, 1}Q_{3, 2} \pmod{x_1}$. 

Likewise, the three forms $x_1 + x_i + x_j$ of $Q_{4, 3}$ become the forms $x_i + x_j$ of $Q_{3, 2}$, and its fourth form is $x_2 + x_3 + x_4 = Q_{3, 3}$; so $Q_{4, 3} \equiv Q_{3, 2}Q_{3, 3} \pmod{x_1}$. Together with $x_2x_3x_4 = Q_{3, 1}$, this gives $\bar F = Q_{3, 3}(Q_{3, 1}Q_{3, 2})^2 = (x_2 + x_3 + x_4)\,m_{(3, 2, 1)}(y)^2$ by \Cref{lem:vdm}.

By \Cref{prp:frob}, $m_{(3, 2, 1)}(y)^2 = \sum_\sigma y^{2\sigma}$, and multiplication by $x_2 + x_3 + x_4$ adds some $\chi_l$ to the exponent. No terms cancel: $2\sigma + \chi_l$ determines $l$ as the place of its only odd entry, and then $\sigma$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label[lemma]{lem:bottom}
Let $q \geq 0$ and $w' \in \mathbb{Z}^3$ with $|w'| = 13$; then $w'$ has one or three odd entries.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
 \item If $w'$ has three odd entries, then $c_{q + 1}(1, w') = 0$.
 \item If $w'$ has one odd entry, at the place $i$, and $u := \frac{w' + \chi_i}{2}$ (that is, $u = \lceil w'/2\rceil$, rounded up entrywise), then
 \[
  c_{q + 1}(1, w') = \sum_\sigma c_q(1, u + \sigma),
 \]
 the sum over the six permutations $\sigma$ of $(1, 2, 3)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
By \Cref{lem:descent}, $c_{q + 1}(1, w')$ is the sum of $c_q(v)$, $v := \frac{(1, w') + \pi}{2}$, over the $\pi \in \operatorname{supp} P$ with $\pi \equiv (1, w') \pmod 2$. Since $x_1$ divides $P$, $c_q(v) \neq 0$ needs the first entry $2^q - v_1$ of $C_q - v$ to be at least $2^q - 1$, that is, $\pi_1 = 1$. By \Cref{lem:x1} such $\pi$ are $(1, 2\sigma + \chi_l)$, and $2\sigma + \chi_l \equiv \chi_l \pmod 2$.

So if $w'$ has three odd entries, no $\pi$ has the parity of $(1, w')$, which proves (a). If $w' \equiv \chi_i \pmod 2$, exactly the six $\pi$ with $l = i$ have it, and for them $v = (1, u + \sigma)$, which proves (b).
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label[corollary]{cor:pair}
Let $q \geq 0$ and $u \in \mathbb{Z}^3$ with $|u| = 7$. If the last two entries of $u$ are equal, then
\[
 c_{q+1}(1,2u-\chi_i)=0,
 \qquad i=1,2,3.
\]
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
The vector $2u - \chi_i$ has its only odd entry at the place $i$, and $\frac{(2u - \chi_i) + \chi_i}{2} = u$. So by \Cref{lem:bottom}(b),
\[
 c_{q + 1}(1, 2u - \chi_i) = \sum_\sigma c_q(1, u + \sigma).
\]
Let $\tau$ exchange the last two entries of a vector in $\mathbb{Z}^3$. Since $\tau u = u$, we have $\tau(u + \sigma) = u + \tau\sigma$, so $\tau$ permutes the six vectors $u + \sigma$; it fixes none of them, because the last two entries of $\sigma$ differ. Hence the six terms split into three pairs $c_q(1, u + \sigma)$, $c_q(1, u + \tau\sigma)$, and the two terms of each pair are equal by \eqref{eq:C-symmetry}. So the sum is even, that is, $0$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label[corollary]{cor:two}
For every $q\geq1$,
\[
 c_q(1,3,6,4)=1,
 \qquad
 c_q(1,6,3,4)=0.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \nu_q:=
 (2^q-1,\;3\cdot2^q-3,\;5\cdot2^q-6,\;5\cdot2^q-4)
 \in\operatorname{supp} P^{2^q-1},
\]
whereas $C_q-(1,6,3,4)\notin\operatorname{supp} P^{2^q-1}$.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
For $w'=(6,3,4)$, \Cref{lem:bottom} gives $u=(3,2,2)$,
so \Cref{cor:pair} yields $c_q(1,6,3,4)=0$ for $q\geq1$.

For the first coefficient, put $u:=(2,3,2)$ and
\[
 s_q:=c_{q + 1}(1, 3, 6, 4) = \sum_\sigma c_q(1,u+\sigma).
\]
The six vectors $u+\sigma$ are
\[
 (3,5,5),\quad(5,5,3),\quad(5,4,4),\quad
 (3,6,4),\quad(4,6,3),\quad(4,4,5).
\]
At level zero only $(3,5,5)$ contributes, so $s_0=1$.
For $q\geq1$, the first two coefficients vanish by
\Cref{lem:bottom}, and the third by \Cref{cor:pair}.
Hence
\[
 s_q=c_q(1,3,6,4)+c_q(1,4,6,3)+c_q(1,4,4,5).
\]
By \Cref{lem:bottom},
\[
 c_q(1,3,6,4)
 =c_q(1,4,5,4)
 =c_q(1,4,6,3)
 =s_{q-1}.
\]
Also $c_q(1,4,4,5)=c_q(1,4,5,4)$ by
\eqref{eq:C-symmetry}. Thus $s_q=3s_{q-1}=s_{q-1}$,
and $s_q=1$ for all $q\geq0$.
Finally, $c_q(1,3,6,4)=s_{q-1}=1$ for $q\geq1$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label[theorem]{thm:T}
Let $j,q\geq1$, and put
\[
 m:=2^{q+1}(2^j-1)+2^q-1,\qquad
 \theta^0:=(R_j,R_j-1,R_j-2,R_j-3),
 \qquad
 T:=2^{q+1}\theta^0+\nu_q.
\]
Then $T\in\operatorname{supp} P^m$ and
\[
 \max_iT_i=T_1=2^{q+1}R_j+2^q-1.
\]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
By the definition of $\nu_q$,
\[
 T=2^{q+1}R_j(1,1,1,1)
   +(2^q-1,\;2^q-3,\;2^q-6,\;-2^q-4),
\]
so $T_1$ is the largest entry.

By Frobenius,
\[
 P^m
 =P^{2^j-1}(x_1^{2^{q+1}},\dots,x_4^{2^{q+1}})
  P^{2^q-1}.
\]
Thus $[x^T]P^m$ is the parity of the number of pairs
\[
 \theta\in\operatorname{supp} P^{2^j-1},\qquad
 \lambda\in\operatorname{supp} P^{2^q-1},\qquad
 2^{q+1}\theta+\lambda=T.
\]
Since $\lambda_i\geq2^q-1$ and
$T_i\leq2^{q+1}R_j+2^q-1$, every $\theta_i\leq R_j$.
By symmetry, \Cref{cor:distinct} and \Cref{thm:lower}(ii),
$\theta$ is a permutation of $\theta^0$.
Write
\[
 a :=\sigma(0,1,2,3), \sigma \in S_4,\qquad
 \theta=R_j(1,1,1,1)-a.
\]
Then
\[
 \lambda=\nu_q+2^{q+1}\bigl(a -(0,1,2,3)\bigr).
\]
The bounds $2^q-1\leq\lambda_i\leq7(2^q-1)$ fix the places of $0$ and $3$ in $a$. If $a_i=0$ for some $i\geq2$, then $\lambda_i$ is $2^q-3$, $2^q-6$, or $-2^q-4$, below the lower bound; so $a_1=0$. If $a_i=3$ for some $i\leq3$, then $\lambda_i$ is $7\cdot2^q-1$, $7\cdot2^q-3$, or $7\cdot2^q-6$, above the upper bound; so $a_4=3$. Hence $a=(0,1,2,3)$ or $a=(0,2,1,3)$.

In the second case,
\[
 \lambda=
 (2^q-1,\;5\cdot2^q-3,\;3\cdot2^q-6,\;5\cdot2^q-4).
\]
This is $C_q-(1,6,3,4)$ with its middle entries exchanged,
so it does not occur by \Cref{cor:two} and symmetry.
The only contributing pair is therefore
$(\theta^0,\nu_q)$, whose two factors occur by
\Cref{thm:AP} and \Cref{cor:two}. Thus $[x^T]P^m=1$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Part~(i) is \Cref{cor:dyadic}.

For part~(ii), put
\[
 a:=2^{q+1}(2^j-1),\qquad b:=a+2^q-1.
\]
By \Cref{cor:double,cor:dyadic},
$d^*(a)=2^{q+1}R_j$.
If $q=0$, then $r=0$ and the claim follows.
For $q\geq1$, \Cref{thm:T} gives
\[
 d^*(b)\leq2^{q+1}R_j+2^q-1=d^*(a)+b-a.
\]
Thus \Cref{cor:interval} yields
\[
 d^*(a+r)=2^{q+1}R_j+r,
 \qquad 0\leq r\leq2^q-1.
\]

For part~(iii), equality holds when $m=2^j-1$ by part~(i).
Otherwise, write $m=2^{q+1}(2^j-1)+r$ as in part~(ii).
Then
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 d^*(m)-R(m,4,3)
 &=3\cdot2^q+r-\left\lceil\frac{7r+3}{2}\right\rceil\\
 &=3\cdot2^q-\left\lceil\frac{5r+3}{2}\right\rceil\\
 &\geq3\cdot2^q-\frac{5r+4}{2}\\
 &\geq\frac{2^q+1}{2}>0,
 \end{aligned}
\]
where the penultimate inequality uses $r\leq2^q-1$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
